newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE-London show focuses on mysterious Seurat masterpiece.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-London show focuses on mysterious Seurat masterpiece.

text.p: The giant painting first saw the light of day in a crowded Parisian beer hall after being rejected by judges at an art show in 1884.
One U.S. newspaper critic described it as the product of "a vulgar, coarse and commonplace mind".
And yet "Bathers at Asnieres", painted by Frenchman Georges Seurat when he was just 24, is now recognised as one of the great late 19th century paintings.

"Bathers" is the focus of a major new exhibition at London's National Gallery, which traces how Seurat prepared himself over the course of a year to produce a work which has both tantalised and troubled critics.
At first sight, it is hardly revolutionary. A small group of men and boys idles in bright sunshine on the bank of the Seine river in a bustling resort just to the north of Paris.
Two boys are in the water up to their waists. The background sky is stained with smoke belching from chimneys in the industrial region of Clichy.
BREAK WITH IMPRESSIONISTS
What critics found particularly unsettling was the aloofness of each character, how none of those portrayed in the picture had any interest in the others.

"By judicious use of colour and texture Seurat coalesced nature and industry, suburb and sunlight, in this manufactured idyll, prising grandeur out of these apparent disjunctions," says a special book published in conjunction with the exhibition.

"In the soft, embracing light of the riverbank, Seurat's bathers seem perfect formal units, and yet in social terms they are isolated and thus imperfect. That tension in what we see, that jarring of the harmony, that imperfection in perfection, is what gives 'Bathers' its sense of mystery."
The painting also marked a break with the dominant Impressionist school of painters, who had rejected the formal classical style in favour of quick, broad brushstrokes and wild explosions of colour.
Seurat placed emphasis once again on an ordered and classical style, one which was much more deliberate, systematic and refined.
He chose a meticulous approach, devouring books on colour theories and studying how to play tones off against each other, as well as the harmony produced by pairs of complementary colours.

"It was a first great public statement. He seemed to be starting off with the bright impressionist approach and combining it with classical form," said Professor John House, deputy director of London's prestigious Courtauld Institute of Art.
"He was trying to create monumental art out of impressionism, which had seemed ephemeral. It was an attempt to be more precise with light and colour," he said in an interview.
SKETCHES INCLUDED IN EXHIBITION
The exhibition, which runs to September 28, includes dozens of preliminary sketches Seurat produced in crayon and oils as well as a series of other paintings through the ages which influenced him.
"'Bathers' is an extremely beautiful painting. One of things which makes it amazing is that it is so perplexing. It works on many levels," said Professor Richard Thomson, the exhibition's curator.
"In order to get to this picture, here is the path he took as an art student, the artists he looked at as young man," he said in an interview, explaining how he had put the exhibition together.
"What choices did he make? What path did he follow? What might he have done and decided against? Those are the questions that the intelligent viewer will be asking."
The 10 black-and-white crayon drawings, spread among private and public collections around the world, have been reunited for first time since Seurat's death at the age of just 31.
BRUSHWORK REVEALED BY X-RAYS
X-rays of the painting show that the artist covered the canvas with layer after layer of paint, using criss-cross strokes for the trees and the grass and horizontal strokes for the water.

"The softly blended mottled colours of the figures' clothes and streaks of bright yellow, orange and blue paint within the overall green of the grass gives a constantly shifting effect. In no area of the painting is simple unmodulated colour used," explains the book which accompanies the exhibition.
Also on show are preliminary studies for later works, produced after Seurat became one of the leading proponents of pointillism -- the art of creating paintings with individual pin-points of colour.
These include one famous painting of La Grande Jatte, the island in the middle of the Seine popular with the middle classes. A tip of the island juts into the far right-hand corner of "Bathers".
SEURAT EXPERIMENTS WITH STYLE
Seurat experimented widely, refusing to restrict himself to any one style, and is generally credited with producing at last seven major works.

"Some of the last pictures were decorative, some of the ways in which his paintings were organised looked forwards to the abstract artists of the 20th century and some were very impressionistic," said House.
Seurat died on March 29, 1891, of infectious angina after catching a chill.
"One of the most frustrating things in the world is not knowing what he could have done had he not died," said House.
"At his funeral a friend said Seurat had his next few pictures already painted in his mind when he died and we don't know what they were."
